name: OpenAI (OpenAI Foundation; OpenAI Group PBC)
subcategory: frontier LLMs (GPT), ChatGPT and API; occasional open-weights releases (GPT-2, gpt-oss)
origin_detail: Founded December 2015 as the non-profit OpenAI, Inc. by Elon Musk, Sam Altman, Ilya Sutskever, Greg Brockman and others; $1B was pledged but only $133M had been received by 2021. In 2019 it added a 'capped' for-profit arm (100x cap). On 2025-10-28 it recapitalised: the non-profit became the OpenAI Foundation, which controls the for-profit OpenAI Group PBC.
openness_notes: Initial 3: a non-profit research lab that promised researchers would 'publish their work, whether as papers, blog posts, or code' and share patents. The 2018-era Charter already expected 'safety and security concerns will reduce our traditional publishing'. GPT-2 was withheld in Feb 2019 and released in stages through Nov 2019, and later frontier models (GPT-3 onward) were API-only. Current 1: the frontier is closed; gpt-oss (2025-08-05) put two capable open-weight models under Apache-2.0, an OSI licence, but these are peripheral to a business built on closed models and subscriptions.

relicensing_events.from: Default open publication of research and code
relicensing_events.to: Staged/withheld release of GPT-2; later models API-only
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Justified by misuse concerns ('malicious applications'); the 1.5B GPT-2 was released on 2019-11-05, but from GPT-3 on the frontier stayed closed.
Followed Altman's Jan 2025 remark, after DeepSeek, that OpenAI needed to 'figure out a different open source strategy'; framed as US-built open models that 'expand democratic AI rails'.

relicensing_events.to: OpenAI Foundation (26% stake, ~$130B, plus warrant) controlling OpenAI Group PBC; Microsoft ~27%
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Governance/ownership change announced 2025-10-28; Musk's suit seeking to reverse it lost in May 2026 on the statute of limitations.

funding_as_of: 2026-04 (rounds include $6.6B Oct 2024 at $157B; $40B Apr 2025 at $300B post; $10B employee sale Oct 2025 at $500B; $110B Feb 2026 at $730B, extended to $122B committed at $852B post-money; total not computed)
risk_events: 2025: net loss of about $9B on $13.1B revenue (estimate in Wikipedia infobox)

Musk v. Altman: Musk sued over the departure from the non-profit mission, amended in April 2026 to seek reversal of the restructuring, and lost in May 2026 (jury found he sued after the three-year statute of limitations)
2026-06-08: confirmed an IPO filing with the SEC; in September Altman said the IPO was delayed until 2027
Ownership split after recapitalisation: the Foundation's stake is 26% (infobox gives 22.5% after later rounds), so the non-profit's control rests on special voting rights rather than majority equity
robustness: Very well funded ($852B post-money valuation in early 2026; $122B committed in its latest round) but loss-making, and dependent on continued capital and compute deals. The non-profit Foundation controls the PBC board through special voting rights. Its open contributions are few but durable: GPT-2 and gpt-oss weights under permissive terms cannot be withdrawn.
physical_science_relevance: OpenAI for Science ('Accelerating scientific discovery') targets mathematics, physics, biology and chemistry; gpt-oss models can be run locally in labs under Apache-2.0.
openness_effect_assessment: OpenAI's founding openness attracted talent and legitimacy, but the decisive commercial step was closing the frontier: from GPT-3 onward API-only access underpinned the ChatGPT business ($13.1B revenue in 2025) and a valuation climb from $157B (Oct 2024) to $852B (2026). Competitive pressure from open models (DeepSeek, Jan 2025) pushed it back to a limited open-weights release (gpt-oss, Aug 2025) without opening its frontier. Its restructuring into a PBC drew litigation that failed but kept the openness-versus-mission question public.
key_takeaway: OpenAI is the archetype of an organisation founded on openness that became closed as its models became valuable. Its name and 2015 pledge to publish code now sit beside an $852B closed-model business, and its one major re-opening (gpt-oss under Apache-2.0) was a response to open-weights competitors rather than a return to its founding model. For the study, it is the clearest example of openness used to launch, then traded for control once capital needs rose, with governance (a non-profit holding special voting rights) kept as the remaining link to the original mission.
